Issued at 1250 PM CST Sun Nov 15 2026

A broad area of high pressure continues to reside across the 
Great Lakes and most of the Midwest this afternoon which will 
continue to promote mostly clear skies through tonight. While 
temperatures will continue to warm into the lower 50s this 
afternoon, once the sun sets temperatures will quickly begin to 
cool back into the 30s before settling into the mid to upper 20s
overnight. The combination of this stout radiational cooling 
and light winds will generate some marginally favorable 
conditions for patchy fog development tonight into early Monday 
morning (20-30% chance). The main limiting factor for the fog 
tonight will be how deep moisture depths get this evening before
mid-level winds increase after midnight and start to mix down 
some drier air. For now have opted to maintain patchy fog in the
official forecast for areas south of I-80 where low-level 
moisture is currently expected to be highest, but also opted to 
extend some fog mention into portions of northwest IL west of 
the Fox Valley where radiational cooling will be strongest. 
Regardless, fog coverage should be rather hit and miss and 
generally shallow which should cap visibilities generally in the
2-4 mile range at worst. However, if fog fails to materialize 
then expect another morning of widespread frost. 

The surface high will begin to shift into the Ohio and 
Tennessee River Valleys on Monday as a modest shortwave pivots 
through the Great Lakes. Given the dry conditions beneath this 
shortwave, no precipitation is expected with the wave but some 
scattered mid-level clouds may be seen Monday afternoon. In the 
wake of this shortwave, mid-level ridging will build across the 
Midwest and Great Lakes which will keep the dry weather around 
through at least the middle of the week. Winds will also turn 
southwesterly and increase a bit which will begin to usher in 
some warmer air. The combination of this warm advection and the 
mostly sunny skies will allow daily temperatures to climb into 
the mid to upper 50s to near 60 by Thursday. Overnight lows 
however, will continue to dip into the 30s Monday and Tuesday 
nights as the dry conditions continue to promote good 
radiational cooling. 

Heading into the later half of the week, the broad trough 
currently off of the Pacific Northwest will move onshore Tuesday
night and then eject across the Mountain West towards the 
northern Plains and Upper Midwest by Wednesday night. At the 
same time, a secondary shortwave trough is forecast to move 
onshore near southern California and eject northeastward along 
the southern periphery of the mainstream trough. Depending on 
the degree of phasing between this secondary shortwave and the 
main trough, this secondary trough could pivot over northern IL 
and the central Great Lakes on Thursday. Initially it looked as 
if this shortwave would bring with it some chances for rain 
showers on Thursday, but recent guidance trends have started to 
back away from this scenario due to a lack of sufficient 
moisture return ahead of the wave. So while an isolated shower 
or two cannot be fully ruled out on Thursday just yet 
(especially in our west/northwest CWA), our current forecast 
will have some silent 10-14% POPs and advertise mostly dry 
conditions. Aside from the rain chances, this shortwave will 
also bring with it some breezy southwest winds as our area 
becomes sandwiched between a surface high over the Mid-Atlantic 
and a deepening surface low over southern Ontario. Thus, expect 
wind gusts on Wednesday and Thursday to be in the 20-30 mph 
range. 

Our next notable chance for rain does not look to arrive until 
next weekend when another trough and associated low pressure 
system drag and cold front through the region. In the wake of 
this cold front, longer range ensemble guidance does show a 
return to more seasonable temperatures with highs more in the 
40s and overnight lows in the 20s and 30s.

Yack
